passages.title: Woe to the defrauders in weights and measures
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat open Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn with a divine declaration of ruin against people who cheat in weights and measures — and then, in a single breathtaking turn, drag the marketplace into the courtroom of the Day of Judgement. What binds the passage together is one argument: ayat 1–3 name the crime, and ayat 4–6 expose its root — a heart that does not truly reckon on standing before the Lord of all the worlds.

## The word that names the crime

The passage begins with *wayl* — "Woe!" — a word Ibn Kathir explains as a promise of **loss and destruction** from Allah Himself. The people it targets are the *muṭaffifīn*, a word derived from *taṭfīf*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as "to give short measure or short weight." The very form of the expression, the commentary notes, carries legal force: "Woe to the curtailers" is not merely a lament but an injunction — this practice is prohibited.

Ayat 2 and 3 then paint the muṭaffif's portrait with devastating precision, and the portrait is one of *asymmetry*. When he is the one receiving — buying, collecting a debt — he demands full measure, and as Ibn Kathir adds, "extra as well" (ayah 2). But when he is the one giving — measuring or weighing out for others — he shaves the scale and gives less than due (ayah 3). Ibn Kathir captures both directions in one definition: taṭfīf is to be stingy with measurement and weight, "either by increasing it if it is due from the others, or decreasing it if it is a debt." The sin, in other words, is not ignorance of fairness. The muṭaffif knows exactly what a full measure looks like — he insists on it whenever it is owed *to* him. His crime is a double standard: one scale for taking, another for giving.

## The moment of revelation

The occasion of these ayat is recorded in the collections of An-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah from Ibn ʿAbbās: "When the Prophet ﷺ came to Al-Madinah, the people of Al-Madinah were the most terrible people in giving measurement (i.e., they used to cheat). Thus, Allah revealed, *Woe to Al-Muṭaffifīn*. After this, they began to give good measure."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the picture. Madinah was a trading town whose transactions ran largely on measurement, and the custom there was exactly the asymmetry the ayat describe: strict and exacting when receiving, careless and cheating when selling. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said this was the first sūrah revealed upon the Prophet's ﷺ arrival in Madinah — and the report (transmitted by Hakim, Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah, with a sound chain as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes) ends with a remarkable testimony: the people abandoned the practice so completely that they became *well-known for honesty* in weighing and measuring. A few verses re-formed the commercial ethics of an entire city.

On the sūrah's dating the early authorities differed, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records both views: Ibn Masʿūd held it was revealed in Makkah — hence most copies of the Qurʼān label it Makkī — while Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, Muqātil and Ḍaḥḥāk held it to be Madanī, with only about eight verses Makkī.

## An old command, and an old destruction

Ibn Kathir stresses that this warning is not new legislation but the reaffirmation of a command running through the whole Qurʼān: "And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a balance that is straight" (17:35); "And give full measure and full weight with justice. We burden not any person, but with that which he can bear" (6:152); "And observe the weight with equity and do not make the balance deficient" (55:9). And history has already shown where the crime leads: Allah destroyed the people of Shuʿayb and wiped them out **because of their cheating in weights and measurements**. The "woe" of ayah 1 is not an empty threat; it has precedent.

## Wider than the marketplace

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out a principle that turns these ayat from a merchants' regulation into a mirror for every life. Weighing and measuring, it argues, are only *instruments* — their whole purpose is to give a person what he deserves. So the prohibition of taṭfīf is not restricted to scales and containers: it covers **every means by which someone's rights are evaluated**, whether by weight, measure, number, or anything else. Giving anyone less than his due, in any currency, is taṭfīf.

The early Muslims understood it exactly this way. It is recorded in the Muwaṭṭaʼ of Imam Malik that ʿUmar Ibn-ul-Khaṭṭāb saw a man cutting short his bowing and prostration in prayer and said to him: "You have committed taṭfīf (curtailed the right) of Allah." Rushed rukūʿ is short-changing — not a customer, but Allah. From this, Imam Malik formulated a postulate: **"Everything has a full due and a short measure."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān applies it across the board: prayer, ablution, cleanliness, all the rights of Allah — and equally the rights of people. Its most pointed modern example is the workplace: an employee contracted for specified hours who curtails them is guilty of taṭfīf. And it adds a sobering observation: people generally — "even scholars" — are lax here, not regarding the curtailment of work obligations as sin at all.

## Why the answer is the Resurrection (ayat 4–6)

Having named the crime, the passage does not respond with a market regulation. It asks a question that goes underneath the behaviour to the belief that permits it: "Do they not think that they will be resurrected, for a tremendous Day — the Day all people will stand before the Lord of all worlds?" (ayat 4–6). Ibn Kathir reads this as a direct threat: do these people not fear standing before **He Who knows the hidden matters and the innermost secrets**, on a Day of great horror and tremendous fright? Whoever loses on *that* Day, he warns, will be made to enter a blazing fire. The logic is piercing: a person cheats over grams and handfuls only because, at some functional level, he is not reckoning on the audit.

The sources then let the Sunnah describe what that "standing" (ayah 6) will actually be. Ibn Kathir says mankind will stand barefooted, naked and uncircumcised, at a station so difficult and distressful for the criminals that strength and senses will not be able to bear it. Imam Malik reported from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ said, commenting on this very ayah: "This will be the Day that mankind will stand before the Lord of all that exists, until one of them will sink up to the middle of his ears in sweat" — a hadith recorded by Al-Bukhari, and by Muslim from two routes. Imam Ahmad recorded from Al-Miqdād that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the sun will be brought within a mile or two of the servants, and people will be submersed in sweat **according to the measure of their deeds** — some up to their heels, some up to their knees, some up to their groins, and some bridled in it up to the neck (recorded also by Muslim and At-Tirmidhi). Notice the fit: those who manipulated measures will themselves be *measured* in that standing, deed for deed.

How long will it last? Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Masʿūd that they will stand forty years, heads raised to the sky, no one speaking, righteous and wicked alike bridled in sweat; and from Ibn ʿUmar, that it will be a hundred years.

And the Prophet ﷺ himself took that Day with such seriousness that, as recorded in Sunan Abu Dawud, he used to seek refuge with Allah from the hardship of standing on the Day of Judgement. In the Sunans of Abu Dawud, An-Nasa'i, and Ibn Majah, ʿĀʼishah relates that he would open his late-night prayer declaring Allah's greatness ten times, praising Him ten times, glorifying Him ten times, seeking forgiveness ten times, then saying: "O Allah! Forgive me, guide me, provide for me, and protect me" — and then seeking refuge from the hardship of that standing.

## What cheating costs a society — here, before the Hereafter

The sources add that taṭfīf is not only punished on the Great Day; it corrodes the world of the cheaters now. Ibn ʿAbbās narrated that the Prophet ﷺ spoke of five sins bringing five punishments, among them: "Those who curtail measures and weights, Allah will cause famine to break out amongst them" (cited by Qurtubi, who said Al-Bazzar narrated its overall sense in different words; Malik Ibn Anas also narrated it from Ibn ʿUmar). Tabarani narrates from Ibn ʿAbbās a similar teaching: "a community that gives short measure and weight, Allah cuts off their sustenance." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that this cutting-off takes many forms — goods may vanish, or exist but sit beyond reach behind unbearable prices; and *faqr*, usually translated "poverty," really means "being in need, dependent on others," so that even a wealthy society strangled by dependence and restriction is living one form of this punishment. A community that short-changes each other finds itself, measure for measure, short-changed in its provision.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with one working question: *where are my two scales?* The standard it sets is simple and searching — the fullness you demand when something is owed to you is exactly the fullness you must give when you owe. In the shop, yes; but by Imam Malik's postulate, also in your prayer, your ablution, your contracted hours of work, and every right anyone holds over you. "Everything has a full due and a short measure" — and the One before whom all people will one day stand, sweating according to their deeds, is the Lord of all worlds, He Who knows the hidden matters and the innermost secrets.

passages.title: The wicked's record in Sijjin and their doom
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah 83, Ayat 7–17: The Record of the Wicked and Their Doom

This passage is the Qurʼān's answer to a question every human being eventually asks: what actually becomes of the wicked? Ayat 7–17 move in one unbroken arc — from the record of their deeds, kept in a place called Sijjīn, to the spiritual disease that made them deniers in the first place, and finally to their doom on the Day of Judgement: a sealed record, a rusted heart, and a screen between them and their Lord.

## What is Sijjīn?

The passage opens in ayah 7 with **kallā** — "But no!", "Never!" — which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān glosses here as: they should never forget that Day. "Truly, the Record of the wicked is in Sijjīn."

The word **Sijjīn** repays attention. As Ibn Kathir notes, it is derived from *sijn*, "prison," and here it means straitened circumstances. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the root verb *sajana* means "to imprison in a narrow place," and cites Qāmūs giving the meaning "eternal imprisonment." So before we are told anything about *where* Sijjīn is, the word itself has already told us *what* it is: a place of crushing narrowness.

Then ayah 8 asks: "And what will make you know what Sijjīn is?" This question is not seeking information — Ibn Kathir explains that with it Allah expresses the greatness of the matter: "a great matter, an eternal prison, and a painful torment."

As for its location, Ibn Kathir cites the lengthy hadith of al-Barāʼ bin ʿĀzib, in which the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah says concerning the soul of the disbeliever, "Record his book in Sijjīn" — and Sijjīn is beneath the seventh earth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same hadith with the contrast it contains: Sijjīn is beneath the seventh level of the earth, while ʿilliyyīn is in the seventh heaven beneath the Divine Throne. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words, "Then We reduced him to the lowest of the low, save those who believe and do righteous deeds" (95:5–6): it is known that the destination of the wicked will be Hell, and it is the lowest of the low. He also cites 25:13 — the wicked "thrown into a narrow place thereof, chained together" — for Sijjīn is full of hardship and misery.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that according to the traditions, Sijjīn is a special place where the souls of the non-believers are kept, and in the same place the record of every wicked person's evil deeds is kept separately — possibly alongside a consolidated book in which the deeds of all the non-believers of the world are recorded. It further cites a narration recorded by Baihaqi from ʿAbdullāh Ibn Salām that Paradise is in the heaven and Hell is in the earth, and a narration cited by Ibn Jarir on the authority of Muʿādh Ibn Jabal in which the Prophet ﷺ, asked from where Hell will be brought forward on that Day (89:23), replied: "From the seventh earth." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this interpretation is reconcilable with narratives that define Sijjīn as the name of a place in Hell — and Allah knows best.

## A register inscribed and sealed

Ayah 9 — "a register inscribed" (*kitābun marqūm*) — needs careful reading, and both commentaries pause over it. This phrase, they explain, is *not* the answer to "what is Sijjīn?" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this point to Imam Baghawi and Ibn Kathir. It describes instead the *record* of the wicked mentioned in ayah 7: a book that is, in Ibn Kathir's words, "inscribed, written, and completed. No one can add to it and no one can remove anything from it" — a statement he relays from Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Qurazi. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *marqūm* ("inscribed") here signifies *makhtūm* — "sealed": no one can add anything to it, nor remove anything from it, nor is any alteration possible in it. The place where this book is kept for safe-custody is Sijjīn, where the souls of the wicked unbelievers are gathered.

There is a quiet irony here: these are people who denied that any reckoning would ever happen — and all the while their record was already inscribed and sealed.

## Who denies — and why

Ayah 10 pronounces the sentence: "Woe, that Day, to the deniers." Ibn Kathir explains that *wayl* ("woe") means destruction and devastation, and he illustrates how seriously the Sunnah treats even lying for laughter with a hadith recorded in the Musnad and the Sunan collections on the authority of Bahz bin Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Woe unto whoever speaks, and lies in order to make the people laugh. Woe unto him, woe unto him." If casual lying earns "woe," what of a lifetime spent calling the Day of Recompense a lie?

Ayat 11–12 then identify the deniers. Ayah 11: they deny the Day of Recompense — Ibn Kathir: they do not believe it will happen and do not believe in its existence; they consider it far-fetched. Ayah 12: "And none can deny it except every transgressor, sinner" (*muʿtadin athīm*). Ibn Kathir draws out the portrait behind these two words: **transgressive in his actions** — doing the forbidden and exceeding the limits even when acquiring the permissible — and **a sinner in his statements** — he lies whenever he speaks, breaks his promises whenever he makes them, and behaves in an abusive and wicked manner whenever he argues. The ayah itself ties the denial to this character: none deny it *except* such a person.

So when the Qurʼān is recited to such a man, ayah 13 tells us his reflex: "Tales of the ancients!" (*asāṭīr al-awwalīn*). Ibn Kathir explains: whenever he hears the Words of Allah from the Messenger ﷺ, he denies it and has ill thoughts about it, believing it to be a collection gathered from the books of the ancients. Ibn Kathir points to the same accusation elsewhere in the Qurʼān — 16:24, and 25:5, where they even alleged that it was written down "and dictated to him morning and afternoon."

## The rust on the heart

Ayah 14 is the spiritual centre of the passage, and both commentaries linger over it: "No! Rather, there has rusted upon their hearts what they used to earn."

Again the ayah opens with **kallā**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that in Arabic grammar this particle is called *harf-ur-radd* — a "particle of disapproval, particle of repelling or averting" — used here to repel the false idea of the ignorant that the Qurʼān is tales of the ancients. Their problem, the ayah declares, is not with the Book; it is with their hearts.

The key word is **rāna**, from *rayn*, meaning rust, dust, or filth. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān offers the arresting image: just as rust consumes iron and turns it into dust, the rust of committing many sins has covered up their hearts and destroyed their innate, inborn capacity to distinguish right from wrong. Their rejection "is not based on any logical or intellectual evidence" — their hearts have become blind. Ibn Kathir makes the same point: the only thing that blocked their hearts from believing was the dark covering cast over them by the many sins and wrongs they committed. He also relays a distinction between three coverings: *rayn* is the dark covering that overcomes the hearts of the disbelievers, the covering of *ghaym* is for the righteous, and the covering of *ghayn* is for those who are near to Allah.

How does the rust form? The Prophet ﷺ told us exactly, in the hadith Ibn Kathir cites from Abu Hurayrah — recorded by Ibn Jarir, At-Tirmidhi, An-Nasaʼi, and Ibn Majah, with At-Tirmidhi grading it "Hasan Sahih": "Verily, when the servant commits a sin, a black spot appears in his heart. If he repents from it, his heart is polished clean. However, if he increases in the sin, the spot will continue to increase. That is the statement of Allah: 'Nay! But on their hearts is the Rān which they used to earn.'" An-Nasaʼi's wording adds the terrifying end-point: if he returns to the sin, the spot will increase "until it overcomes his (entire) heart, and this is the Rān."

No one wakes up a denier. The heart darkens one unrepented sin at a time, until the organ meant to recognise truth can no longer see it. The phrase "what they used to *earn*" seals the point: the rust is not something done *to* them; it is their own accumulated wage.

## Veiled from their Lord — and what that proves

Ayah 15 announces a punishment that is not fire: "No! Surely, on that Day they will be veiled from their Lord."

Ibn Kathir explains: they will have a place on the Day of Judgement, and lodging in Sijjīn — and along with this, they will be veiled from seeing their Lord and Creator on the Day of Judgement. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this as the recompense for their conduct: they failed to recognise Allah in this world, so the unbelievers will remain deprived of seeing their Lord on the Day of Judgement, and a screen will fall between them and their Lord.

From this ayah the great imams drew a luminous inference. Ibn Kathir records that Imam Abu ʿAbdullāh Ash-Shāfiʿi said: "In this Ayah is a proof that the believers will see Him (Allah), the Mighty and Sublime, on that Day." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes the same argument to Imams Shāfiʿi and Mālik: if being screened off from Allah is singled out as a punishment for the unbelievers, the wording would have "no real sense" unless the believers and friends of Allah are able to see Him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a "Special Note" from some of the learned predecessors that deepens the ayah further: it is proof that man, by virtue of his innate nature, loves Allah. Even the unbelievers, however deeply steeped in false beliefs about His Being and attributes, carry in their hearts a common denominator — they love, respect, and honour Allah, and worship according to their own belief systems in quest of Him and His pleasure; having taken the wrong road, they cannot reach the destination, but they are seeking the same destination of truth. And this is precisely why the veiling is named among their punishments: if a person had no desire to see his Lord, being deprived of that sight would be no punishment at all. The screen wounds them *because* the longing is real.

## The Fire, and the final word

Ayat 16–17 complete the doom, and Ibn Kathir is careful to show that it is cumulative. Ayah 16: "Then verily, they will indeed enter the burning flame of Hell" — along with being prevented from seeing the Most Gracious, they will also be among the people of the Fire.

And then, ayah 17, the last torment — words: "Then it will be said to them: 'This is what you used to deny!'" Ibn Kathir explains that this will be said by way of scolding, rebuking, belittling, and humiliation. The passage that began with their mockery of revelation — "Tales of the ancients!" — closes with them as the object of the rebuke. They spent their lives calling the truth a lie; now the truth stands before them, and they are made to hear it.

## Living it

The passage carries one urgent, practical teaching, and the Prophet ﷺ himself stated it in the hadith of the black spot: the heart is *polishable*. In An-Nasaʼi's wording, the servant who refrains from the sin, seeks forgiveness, and repents finds his heart polished clean — every single time. The rust of ayah 14 overwhelms the heart only when sins are repeated and left unrepented until the spot overcomes it entirely. So the believer's discipline is simple and non-negotiable: do not let any sin sit. Repent quickly, seek forgiveness, and do not return — because what is at stake, this passage teaches, is nothing less than the heart's ability to recognise truth in this world, and the sight of Allah in the next.

passages.title: The righteous in Illiyyun and their bliss
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the sunlit counterpart to the darkness that came before it. The record of the wicked lies in Sijjīn — beneath the seventh earth, as the reports cited here describe it — and, as ayah 15 declared, "Nay! Surely, they will be veiled from seeing their Lord that Day." Now, in ayat 18–28, everything is deliberately reversed: the record of the righteous is kept in the highest heights, witnessed by those nearest to Allah, and its owners are seated on couches, gazing — their faces glowing, their cup sealed with musk. Ibn Kathir opens his commentary on these verses by saying precisely this: "These people are in a situation that is the opposite of the wicked people," and that their final destination, ʿIlliyyīn, is the opposite of Sijjīn. Reading the two halves together is the key to the whole passage.

## ʿIlliyyīn: the register kept on high (ayat 18–21)

Ayah 18 opens with *kallā* — "But no!" — before announcing: the record (*kitāb*) of the *abrār*, the righteous believers, is in ʿIlliyyīn.

What is ʿIlliyyīn? The word itself carries the answer. As both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān note, it is taken from *ʿuluww*, meaning "highness"; some authorities treat it as the plural of *ʿuluww*, signifying "the highest point." Al-Farrāʼ held that it is actually the name of a place — not a true plural, but a word cast on the measure of a plural. Ibn Kathir draws out the image beautifully: the more something ascends and rises, the greater it becomes. That is why ayah 19 asks, "And what will make you realize what ʿIlliyyūn is?" — by this question, Allah magnifies its affair and extols its matter.

The early authorities located it concretely. Ibn Kathir relates (through Hilāl bin Yasāf) that Ibn ʿAbbās once asked Kaʿb about Sijjīn and ʿIlliyyīn in his presence. Kaʿb replied that Sijjīn is the seventh earth, containing the souls of the disbelievers, and ʿIlliyyīn is the seventh heaven, containing the souls of the believers — and others have said the same, that it is the seventh heaven. In another report, via ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah, Ibn ʿAbbās said of this verse: "This means Paradise." Others besides him have said that ʿIlliyyīn is located at Sidrat al-Muntahā, the lote-tree in the upper realm. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites the lengthy traceable Tradition of the Companion Ibn ʿĀzib (may Allah be pleased with him), discussed earlier under Sijjīn, as proof that ʿIlliyyīn is a place in the seventh heaven beneath the Divine Throne where the souls of the believers and their registers of deeds are kept. These positions are not really at odds: the seventh heaven, the lote-tree, and Paradise converge in the upper realm, as we will see below.

Ayah 20 then describes this record: *kitābun marqūm*, "a register inscribed." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a precise point here: this phrase is not an interpretation of ʿIlliyyīn itself, but an explication of the righteous people's records of deeds.

Ayah 21 adds: *yash-haduhu al-muqarrabūn* — "witnessed by those nearest." Who are they? Ibn Kathir records Qatādah's answer: the angels. Ibn ʿAbbās (via al-ʿAwfī) said: "Those nearest to Allah in each heaven will witness it." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the language: the verb *yash-hadu* comes from *shuhūd*, which spans "to attend, to witness, to be present, to observe." On the first reading — which al-Qurṭubī gives — the record of the righteous is in the custody of the angels who are blessed with nearness to Allah. But if *shuhūd* is taken as "being present," the pronoun refers to ʿIlliyyīn rather than to the register, and *al-muqarrabūn* are then the righteous people themselves: their souls are present in ʿIlliyyīn, just as Sijjīn is the abode of the unbelievers.

## Where do souls go after death?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supports that second reading with striking evidence. In the hadith of ʿAbdullāh Ibn Masʿūd recorded in Muslim, the Prophet ﷺ said that the souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds, enjoying the rivers and gardens of Paradise, and their abode is lamps suspended from the Divine Throne — beneath the Throne, yet free to stroll in Paradise. The Qurʼān itself hints at this immediacy in the story of Ḥabīb Najjār in Sūrah Yā Sīn: no sooner had he died than he was told, "Enter the Garden!" (36:26). And this is not only for martyrs: Kaʿb Ibn Mālik narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said, "The soul of a believer is a bird that will be hanging in the tree of Paradise, until it returns to its body on the Day of Judgment" — recorded by Mālik and al-Nasāʼī through an authentic chain, with a similar Tradition of Umm Hāniʼ in the Musnad of Aḥmad and in al-Ṭabarānī.

But other narrations say the souls of the dead remain in their graves — in the lengthy Tradition of Ibn ʿĀzib, the believer's soul is carried up to the sky, Allah commands, "Keep the record of deeds of this servant of Mine in ʿIlliyyūn and return him to the earth, because I have created him from earth, and to it I shall return him, and from it I shall resurrect him," and the angels return the soul to the grave. Imam ʿAbdul Barr preferred this view. How do the reports fit together?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān resolves most of the apparent tension geographically. The Qurʼān says Paradise — Jannat al-Maʼwā — lies "by sidrat-ul-muntahā" (53:14–15), and ahadith confirm the lote-tree is in the seventh heaven. So ʿIlliyyīn, the seventh heaven beneath the Throne, is the very locale of Paradise; souls kept there roam its gardens, so it is equally true to say they are "in Paradise." Likewise Sijjīn lies beneath the seventh earth, where Hell is, so the souls of the disbelievers there receive its heat and torment. As for the grave narrations, Qāḍī Thanāʼullāh Pānīpatī offers a reconciliation in his Tafsīr Maẓharī: ʿIlliyyīn and Sijjīn are the real abodes of the souls, yet each soul retains a special connection with its grave whose nature only Allah knows — just as the sun and moon are in the sky while their light and heat reach the earth. He further distinguishes two aspects of the soul: the subtle substance permeating the body (the *nafs*), which after death is taken up to the heaven and then returned to the grave, where it is rewarded or punished; and the pure, abstract soul — the "soul of the soul" — which remains in ʿIlliyyīn or Sijjīn. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out these views and closes as the scholars themselves do: and Allah knows best. What every report agrees on is the essential point of ayah 18 — the believer's destiny, from the moment of death, is *upward*.

## The bliss itself — and its summit (ayat 22–24)

Ayah 22 turns from the record to its reward: "Surely the virtuous will be in bliss (*naʿīm*)." Ibn Kathir explains: on the Day of Judgement they will be in eternal pleasure, and gardens containing comprehensive bounties. Ayah 23 seats them "on couches (*al-arāʼik*), gazing" — thrones beneath canopies, says Ibn Kathir, from which they will be gazing.

Looking at what? Ibn Kathir transmits two explanations. One: they gaze at their kingdom — at the good and the bounties Allah has given them, which will never end or perish. The other: "they will be looking at Allah, the Mighty and Sublime." Ibn Kathir anchors this second reading in the structure of the sūrah itself: ayah 15 said of the wicked, "Nay! Surely, they will be veiled from seeing their Lord that Day." The righteous are described as the exact opposite — thus, he says, it has been mentioned that they will be allowed to look at Allah while upon their thrones and elevated couches. On this reading the symmetry is complete: the wicked's deprivation is the veil; the righteous's delight is the sight.

Ayah 24 says you will recognize on their faces *naḍrat al-naʿīm* — the glow, the brightness, of delight. Ibn Kathir unpacks the phrase: when you look at them you will notice a radiance that speaks of opulence, decorum, happiness, composure, and authority. Joy that deep cannot be hidden; it shines from the face.

## The sealed cup (ayat 25–28)

Ayah 25: "They will be given a drink of sealed, pure wine" — *raḥīq makhtūm*. Ibn Kathir explains that they will be given drink from the wine of Paradise; Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah and Ibn Zayd all said that *raḥīq* is one of the names of the wine of Paradise.

Ayah 26: "sealed with musk" — *khitāmuhu misk*. Ibn Masʿūd explained: it will be mixed with musk. Ibn ʿAbbās (via al-ʿAwfī) pictured it exquisitely: Allah will give the wine a pleasant aroma for them, and the last thing He places in it will be musk — so the cup is sealed with musk, and the final note as you finish the drink is its finest. Qatādah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same.

Ayat 27–28 add the crowning touch: the drink's mixture comes from *Tasnīm*, "a spring from which those nearest to Allah will drink." Abū Ṣāliḥ and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said Tasnīm is the most excellent and exalted drink of the people of Paradise. And here the passage quietly reveals that Paradise itself has ranks: according to Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās, Masrūq, Qatādah and others, the *muqarrabūn* — those nearest to Allah — drink from Tasnīm pure, as they wish, while the companions of the right hand receive a drink merely *mixed* with it. Even in bliss, nearness has degrees.

## "So let the competitors compete" (ayah 26)

In the middle of this description Allah plants the passage's one command: *wa fī dhālika falyatanāfas al-mutanāfisūn* — "for this let those strive who want to strive." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the word: *tanāfus* means striving to gain some desirable thing before others can get it — the drive behind every race for wealth and position. The verse redirects that very instinct. People compete furiously for material blessings that are perishable; the Qurʼān says: do not make them the goal of life. Be content with what suffices for this fleeting period — if some worldly means is lost, it is not a loss beyond recovery. But for the blessings of Paradise, perfect and eternal in every dimension — *there* let people of aspiration race and outdo one another. Ibn Kathir hears the same note: let the competitors compete and race toward the likes of this, just as Allah says elsewhere, "For the like of this let the workers work" (37:61). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān seals the point with a couplet of the poet Akbar: "Gain and loss — what fiction is this?... Say to the mind, the life is little. If you wish to remind me, remind me of Allah."

That is the practical heart of these eleven ayat. Set beside the wicked — their record in the depths, a veil between them and their Lord — the righteous are shown everything ambition is actually for: a record kept beneath the Throne, a face made radiant, a cup sealed with musk, and, as it has been mentioned, the sight of their Lord from their elevated couches. Whoever must race, let him race for that.

passages.title: The mockers of believers mocked in return
passages.tafsir:
# The Mockers Mocked in Return (83:29–36)

These closing ayat of Sūrah al-Muṭaffifīn set two scenes side by side: the guilty ones laughing at the believers in this world, and the believers laughing at them on the Day of Judgement. What binds the passage together is a single word — laughter — which opens the scene in ayah 29 and returns, reversed, in ayah 34: every ounce of contempt poured on the believers is repaid in full.

## Anatomy of contempt (ayat 29–32)

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah here informs us how "the criminals used to laugh at the believers in the worldly life" — meaning they would mock them and despise them. Maarif ul Quran adds that in these verses Allah depicts fully the attitude of the followers of falsehood towards the upholders of truth. Notice how the passage does not stop at a general statement; it traces the mockery through four distinct moments, each introduced in its own ayah:

**The open laugh (ayah 29).** The mockery begins face to face: those who committed crimes laughed at those who believed.

**The wink in passing (ayah 30).** Whenever they passed by the believers, "they would wink at each other about them," as Ibn Kathir puts it, "in contempt of them."

**The performance at home (ayah 31).** When they returned to their own people, they would return jesting, pleased with themselves. Maarif ul Quran paints the scene: they would take great pleasure in recounting the mocking way they had treated the poor believers, saying that Muhammad ﷺ had misled the simpletons. Ibn Kathir draws out a sharper irony in this ayah. These people went home to comfort — "whatever they request, they find it." Yet with all that ease, "they still are not grateful for Allah's favor upon them. Rather they busy themselves with despising and envying the believers." Ingratitude and mockery grew from the same root: absorbed in belittling others, they never turned to thank the One who was providing for them.

**The confident verdict (ayah 32).** Finally the mockery dresses itself up as judgement: "Verily, these have indeed gone astray!" Ibn Kathir notes the emptiness of the charge — they called the believers misguided simply "because they are upon a religion other than their own religion." The mockers appointed themselves judges of guidance, with no standard but their own way of life.

## "They were not sent as watchers over them" (ayah 33)

Ayah 33 answers that self-appointed judgement with quiet devastation. Ibn Kathir explains: these criminals "have not been sent as guardians over the deeds and statements of these believers. These wrongdoers have not been made responsible for them. So, why are they so concerned with them, and why have they made them the focus of their attention?" No one commissioned the mockers to audit anyone's faith. Their obsession with the believers was not a duty; it was a choice — and a revealing one. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words elsewhere in the Qur'an (23:108–111), where the people of the Fire are told: "But you took them for a laughing stock, so much so that they made you forget My remembrance while you used to laugh at them! Verily, I have rewarded them this Day for their patience: they are indeed the ones that are successful." Mockery of the righteous is not a harmless pastime; in that passage it is what distracted its practitioners from the remembrance of Allah until it ruined them.

## The Day the laughter changes sides (ayat 34–35)

Then comes the turn: *fa-l-yawma* — "but this Day," which Ibn Kathir identifies as the Day of Judgement. On that Day "those who believe will laugh at the disbelievers," and he explains it precisely: "as retribution for how those people laughed at them." The scene is measured, not chaotic — a like-for-like recompense, laughter answered with laughter.

Ayah 35 places the believers "on thrones, looking." Ibn Kathir gives this "looking" a meaning far greater than merely watching the fate of their old tormentors: they will be "looking at Allah, as reward for bearing the false claims against them that they were misguided. They were not misguided at all. Rather they were the close Awliyā' of Allah" — His close friends — "who will be looking at their Lord in the place of His honor." So the answer to the taunt of ayah 32 is complete. The people branded "astray" turn out to be the intimates of Allah, and their reward is fitted exactly to their trial: they were accused of losing their way, and they end by beholding the very Lord they were mocked for following.

## The closing question (ayah 36)

The sūrah ends with a question: "Have not the disbelievers been paid for what they used to do?" Ibn Kathir unfolds it: will the disbelievers be recompensed for their mockery and belittlement of the believers, or not? The question expects only one answer — "they surely will be paid in full, completely and perfectly."

## Living it

Maarif ul Quran refuses to leave this passage in the past. Its author observes that people careless of religion and the Hereafter treat the scholars and the righteous today exactly as the disbelievers once treated the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them — and he prays that Allah rescue the Muslims from this painful scourge. Then he draws out the passage's gift to the one on the receiving end: "There is much solace in this verse for the righteous believers. Never bother about their laughter and mockery." He seals the point with a poet's line: "So long as we fear people's laughter at us, the people will continue laughing at us." The believer who knows how this story ends — thrones, the sight of his Lord, and the last laugh — can walk past the winks and the jokes without flinching. Fear of ridicule only feeds it; certainty in Allah's promise starves it.
